prose_changes.old: The condemnation ended quietism as a movement inside Catholicism, but not the texts. Guyon's writings had a long second life among Protestants — translated, reprinted and read warmly by Pietists, Quakers and Methodists. So that a condemned French Catholic widow became devotional reading in English-speaking evangelicalism, and still is. Fénelon's Telemachus and his letters of spiritual direction stayed in print and are read to this day. The word 'quietism' itself survived as a term of criticism for any spirituality thought too passive.
prose_changes.new: The condemnation ended quietism as a movement inside Catholicism, but not its books. They had a long second life among Protestants. In 1687 the young August Hermann Francke put Molinos's Spiritual Guide into Latin; he later led German Pietism. Quaker booksellers sold Molinos, and a Quaker memoir of 1821 still listed Guyon's Life and Short Method. John Wesley at first called Guyon a 'poor Quietist'. By 1770 he praised her 'excellent piety', and in 1776 he wrote a preface for a short Life of her. So a condemned French Catholic widow became a devotional author for English-speaking evangelicals, and still is. Fénelon's Telemachus and his letters of spiritual guidance stayed in print and are still read. The word 'quietism' lived on too, as a charge against any prayer thought too passive.
prose_changes.reason: 'Guyon's writings ... read warmly by Pietists' is not supported: the vendored Pietist evidence is Francke's Latin translation of Molinos, not Guyon. 'Read warmly' by Methodists overstates Wesley's mixed reading (critical in 1742, admiring by 1770). Rewritten to what the three links document; every other sentence kept.

prose_changes.old: The house was destroyed and the movement formally beaten, yet almost nothing about it actually disappeared. Pascal's Provincial Letters and Pensées became permanent French classics, and the Port-Royal schools' methods, along with the Port-Royal Logic and Grammar, shaped European education for generations. The quarrel outlived the abbey too: Jansenism became a political force in eighteenth-century France and fed the campaign that suppressed the Jesuits, and it produced one lasting institution. The small Church of Utrecht in the Netherlands, which consecrated its own archbishop without Rome in the 1720s and became the root of the Old Catholic churches. The abbey ruins and the farm beside them are now a French national museum.
prose_changes.new: The house was destroyed and the movement formally beaten, yet almost nothing about it truly vanished. Pascal's Provincial Letters and Pensées became lasting French classics. The Port-Royal schools' methods, with the Port-Royal Logic and Grammar, shaped how Europe taught for generations. The quarrel outlived the abbey too. Jansenism became a political force in France in the 1700s. Historians hold that it helped drive the campaign that suppressed the Jesuits. It also left one lasting body: the small Church of Utrecht in the Netherlands. That church made its own archbishop without Rome in the 1720s and became the root of the Old Catholic churches. The abbey ruins and the farm beside them are now a French national museum.

prose_changes.old: The Camisards left no church of their own — French Protestantism rebuilt itself without them, in a completely different key, sober and clandestine. What the prophets left was a wave that carried. The exiles in London published sworn accounts of their experiences, drew crowds and ridicule, and shaped English and continental arguments about religious enthusiasm for a generation, with echoes reaching later revival movements. In the Cévennes the memory was never allowed to fade, and it is still marked by an assembly held every September at the Musée du Désert.
prose_changes.new: The Camisards left no church of their own. French Protestantism rebuilt itself without them, in a wholly different key, sober and hidden. What the prophets left was a wave that carried. The exiles in London published sworn accounts of what they had seen, and drew crowds and scorn. For a generation they shaped the debate in England and Europe over religious enthusiasm. Faint echoes may have reached later revivals: in 1739 John Wesley went to hear a woman 'commonly called' a French prophet. In the Cévennes the memory was never allowed to fade. Every September an assembly still gathers at the Musée du Désert to mark it.
